concept.name: Spot rate curve
concept.definition: The curve of yields on zero-coupon instruments across maturities — the set of rates at which a single future cash flow is discounted to today. It is built by bootstrapping coupon-bearing bond prices so that each instrument is repriced without error, and it is the curve used for present-value calculations.
concept.intuition: Instead of one blended yield per bond, the spot curve gives a separate 'pure' interest rate for every single future date, like a price tag for money delivered at each point in time.
concept.mechanics: Starting from the shortest maturity, each bond's price is decomposed into its cash flows; the discount rate that prices each successive maturity's cash flow exactly (given already-solved shorter rates) is the spot rate for that maturity. The U.S. Treasury bootstraps instantaneous forward rates from on-the-run prices, which equivalently determines the spot curve; Treasury does not publish a daily zero-coupon curve itself.
concept.formula: P = sum over t of CF_t / (1 + z_t)^t, where z_t is the t-year spot (zero-coupon) rate, CF_t the cash flow at time t, and P the bond's price.
concept.failure_modes: The bootstrapped curve depends on the fitting/interpolation method and the input securities chosen, so different constructions give different spot rates, especially between quoted maturities and at the long end.
concept.misconceptions: Spot rates are not directly observable in coupon-bond markets and are not the same as par yields; the par yield curve and the spot curve differ whenever the curve is not flat.
concept.example: If the 2-year spot rate is 4.2%, a single $100 payment due in exactly 2 years is worth 100 / (1.042)^2 ≈ $92.10 today.
